newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Kabul University reopens without women, funds.
newsitem.headline: Kabul University reopens without women, funds.

text.p: Kabul University re-opened on Sunday without women teachers or students, and suffering from an acute shortage of funds and teachers.
The university was closed in September when the purist Islamic Taleban took over Kabul.

For almost four years the university was on the front line between Afghanistan's warring factions: its facilities were destroyed or looted, most of its teaching staff fled abroad, and the young men who scurried between its buildings were carrying Kalashnikov rifles rather than books.
Since the front line moved away two years ago, attempts have been made to rehabilitate the institution, but it is still facing numerous problems.

The re-opening ceremony was held in the university's auditorium. Outside, a young bearded fighter armed with a bayonet and a light machine gun guarded the door; inside, a hole blasted in the roof by a rocket dripped water on the audience and power for the amplification system was provided by an ageing Soviet-built generator.
For most of the speakers, Islam seemed of greater concern than education.

"Even if a man is a doctor or an engineer, if his acts are not based on Islam and Islamic law, he is not a human being." Abul Shoukoor Haqqani, the deputy Minister for Religious Trust, told the gathering.
However, for the rector of the university, the primary worry was to keep it operating.
"We need immediate help to keep the university functioning," said the rector Amir Shah Hassanyar after the ceremony.
"We need stationery, food for the student dormitories, qualified teachers and the money to pay them." he said.
Hassanyar told reporters that 14 faculties would be re-opening with 300 teachers.
"Fourteen faculties will be re-opening; in total 52 departments. We had 360 teachers but 60 of them were women, so we now have 300." he said.

The Taleban have banned women from working except in the medical sector. Female students have also been banned from educational establishments. The Taleban Minister of Higher Education said that the ban on women teachers and students was temporary, but that they would only be allowed back into certain faculties.

"The main problem is a lack of resources. We need separate facilities for girls and we do not have enough women teachers, but if we get the resources women's faculties in certain subjects will be allowed to open," said Maulawi Hamdullah Noumani.
"Although they may not be allowed to study engineering for example, they will be allowed to study medicine, home economics and teaching," he said.
According to Hassanyar, women made up 4,000 of the university's 10,000-strong student body before it was closed.
"In September we had 10,000 students, 6,000 boys and 4,000 girls. We expect about 5,000 students to come back," he said.
Hassanyar also said that finding and retaining qualified teaching staff was proving difficult.

"More than 100,000 Afghan intellectuals have fled abroad in the last 20 years. It is difficult to find 100 people in Afghanistan with a masters degree or a PhD." said Hassanyar, who himself has a doctorate in Ecology from Colorado University in the U.S.

"I am trying to keep in touch with the intellectuals who have stayed. I see little chance of those who fled to the United States and Germany returning in the short term, and if those that remain leave, it would be a catastrophe for Afghanistan," he said.
He said salaries for teaching staff ranged between 700,000 Afghanis ($35) a month for himself to 200,000 Afghanis ($10) for an ordinary teacher.

"For many teachers, their salary is equal to the price of one sack of flour. Most of them have to take second and third jobs. Also many of them have not been out of Afghanistan for 20 years and are totally unaware of developments that have taken place in the world," he said.
